# Go Go Gaia

> Go Go Gaia is an all-in-one women's health tracking app for iOS, made by Holland Neurotech Inc. It covers cycle tracking, pregnancy, postpartum, PCOS, perimenopause, endometriosis, IVF, fertility, symptoms, mood, habits, and nutrition in one dashboard. The website publishes comparison guides, app reviews, and educational content on women's health topics.

## About the company

- App: Go Go Gaia (iOS)
- Company: Holland Neurotech Inc.
- Website: https://www.go-go-gaia.com/
- App Store: https://apps.apple.com/app/apple-store/id6608432371?pt=127249655&ct=llms&mt=8
- Contact: support@hollandneurotech.com
- About page: https://www.go-go-gaia.com/about.html

## Comparison guides (tested, side-by-side reviews)

- [How to choose a period tracker app](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/how-to-choose-period-tracker-app.html): Step-by-step guide comparing Clue, Flo, Ovia and 3 other period trackers across accuracy, privacy, features, and price.
- [Best pregnancy app 2026](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/best-pregnancy-tracking-app.html): Flo, Ovia, What to Expect, BabyCenter and others tested side-by-side on symptom tracking, accuracy, privacy, and community.
- [Clue vs Flo](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/clue-vs-flo.html): Head-to-head comparison of the two most popular period trackers on prediction accuracy, privacy, features, and price.
- [Best fertility app 2026](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/best-fertility-tracking-app.html): Apps compared on ovulation prediction, BBT logging, fertile window accuracy, and TTC tools.
- [Best IVF tracking app 2026](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/best-ivf-tracking-app.html): Apps tested for medication reminders, cycle tracking, and IVF-specific features.
- [Best PCOS tracking app 2026](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/best-pcos-tracking-app.html): Apps for irregular cycles, symptom tracking, and PCOS management.
- [Best perimenopause app 2026](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/best-perimenopause-tracking-app.html): Apps for hot flash logging, HRT tracking, and perimenopause symptoms.
- [Best endometriosis tracking app 2026](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/best-endometriosis-tracking-app.html): Apps for pain logging, flare tracking, and surgery recovery.
- [Best chronic symptom tracker app for women](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/best-symptom-tracker-app-women.html): Apps tested for PMDD, endometriosis, and PCOS symptom tracking.
- [Best PMDD tracking app 2026](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/best-pmdd-tracking-app.html): 7 apps compared for charting PMDD symptoms and mood across cycles, including Me v PMDD, Daylio, Bearable, Clue, Stardust, and Flo. Covers the two-cycle daily charting needed for a diagnosis.
- [Best ovulation tracker app 2026](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/best-ovulation-tracker-app.html): 6 apps compared for finding the fertile window, including Premom, Natural Cycles, Clearblue Connected, Flo, and Ovia Fertility. Covers LH test reading, temperature confirmation, irregular cycles, and at-home hormone monitors like Mira, Inito, Oova, and Tempdrop.
- [Best postpartum and newborn tracking app 2026](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/best-postpartum-tracking-app.html): Apps compared for the fourth trimester, including Huckleberry, Nara Baby, Glow Baby, and Canopie. Covers newborn feeding and sleep tracking plus the mother's own recovery, mood, and return to cycle tracking.
- [Flo vs Natural Cycles](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/flo-vs-natural-cycles.html): Head-to-head on the difference that matters: Flo is a cycle tracker not cleared for contraception, while Natural Cycles is FDA-cleared hormone-free birth control based on basal body temperature. Compared on accuracy, cost, privacy, and what each is actually for.
- [Best birth control and pill reminder app 2026](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/best-birth-control-reminder-app.html): 6 apps compared for staying on birth control, including Natural Cycles, Flo, Medisafe, MyTherapy, and myPill. Separates pill reminder apps from FDA-cleared app-based contraception (only Natural Cycles), with a privacy focus and notes on Spot On, Bedsider, and the shelved Clue Birth Control.
- [Clue vs Natural Cycles](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/clue-vs-natural-cycles.html): Head-to-head on the difference that matters: Clue is a science-first period tracker (Berlin-based, GDPR) not cleared for contraception, while Natural Cycles is FDA-cleared hormone-free birth control based on basal body temperature. Explains what happened to the shelved Clue Birth Control product, and compares the two on privacy, accuracy, irregular cycles, and price.
- [Flo vs Go Go Gaia](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/flo-vs-go-go-gaia.html): Honest head-to-head between Flo, the most-used focused period tracker (huge community, largest content library, iOS and Android), and Go Go Gaia, an all-in-one tracker (cycle plus mood, sleep, nutrition, fitness, habits, wearable sync, iOS only). Compares scope, community, privacy, and price, and is upfront that Flo is the better fit for many readers.
- [Clue vs Flo vs Natural Cycles](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/clue-vs-flo-vs-natural-cycles.html): Three-way comparison of the two leading cycle trackers and the FDA-cleared app-based contraception option, with dedicated free-version, privacy, and irregular-cycle comparisons plus a note on Stardust.
- [Flo vs Ovia](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/flo-vs-ovia.html): Pregnancy-angle head-to-head covering the March 2026 Ovia consolidation, community support for pregnancy questions, and whether Flo Premium is worth it against Ovia's employer-benefit model.
- [Flo alternatives](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/flo-alternatives.html): What happened in the 2025 Flo privacy verdict, an honest case for staying, and seven alternatives compared, including private local-only options.
- [Ovia alternatives](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/ovia-alternatives.html): What changed in Ovia's March 2026 app consolidation, when staying makes sense, and five alternatives matched to different needs.
- [My Mood Wrapped alternatives](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/my-mood-wrapped-alternatives.html): Four apps compared for mood recaps and reviews: Daylio, How We Feel, Bearable, and Go Go Gaia (whose Health Wrapped runs every quarter and scores physical, mental, sleep, and hormonal health together, not just mood).

## Question answers (what women ask, with citable tables)

- [Is it PMS or PMDD?](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/pms-vs-pmdd.html): How to tell PMS from PMDD across severity, timing, functional impact, and what cycle charting reveals.
- [Why is my period late when I'm not pregnant?](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/why-is-my-period-late.html): Common non-pregnancy causes of a late period and a late-period-vs-early-pregnancy comparison.
- [Implantation bleeding vs your period](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/implantation-bleeding-vs-period.html): Table-first comparison across color, timing, duration, flow, and cramping.
- [Can you get pregnant on your period?](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/can-you-get-pregnant-on-your-period.html): Why it is unlikely but possible, with a timeline of the fertile window relative to bleeding.
- [How accurate are period tracker apps?](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/how-accurate-are-period-tracker-apps.html): Accuracy by method (calendar, symptom, BBT, LH, wearable) and why predictions drift for irregular cycles.
- [How to balance your hormones](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/how-to-balance-your-hormones.html): What research actually supports across sleep, exercise, food, and stress, what lacks evidence (seed cycling), and when symptoms warrant a doctor.

## Cycle data explainers (what wearables measure, with cited research)

- [Your hormone curve, explained: estrogen, progesterone & LH](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/hormone-curve-across-your-cycle.html): Phase-by-phase reference for the hormone mechanics underneath every signal a wearable reads. Estrogen climbs and peaks, LH surges, progesterone takes over the luteal phase.
- [HRV and resting heart rate across your cycle](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/hrv-resting-heart-rate-cycle.html): HRV tends to fall and resting heart rate tends to rise in the luteal phase, both driven by progesterone. Covers how much they typically shift and why a single rough night on a ring or watch is not meaningful.
- [Exercise heart rate and training load across your cycle](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/exercise-heart-rate-training-load-cycle.html): Why the same workout can post a different heart rate depending on cycle phase, and why perceived effort often does not shift the same way the number does.
- [Why activity and step count shift across your cycle](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/step-count-activity-cycle-phases.html): Step counts tend to peak in the follicular phase and dip before menstruation even when scheduled workout time barely changes.
- [Blood sugar patterns across your menstrual cycle](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/blog/blood-glucose-cycle-phases.html): CGM research finds glucose runs lower in the late-follicular phase and higher in the luteal phase. Describes the population-level pattern, not an individual target.

## Metrics Encyclopedia (definition-first, citation-checked entries)

- [Metrics Encyclopedia hub](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/): Every metric Go Go Gaia tracks, defined and sourced: biometrics, cycle and fertility terms, hormones and lab analytes, and symptoms. Each entry states what the metric measures, how it's measured, what population-level research shows (with verified citations), and how the app tracks it.
- [Heart rate variability (HRV)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/hrv.html): Beat-to-beat variation reflecting autonomic nervous system activity, measured overnight by wearables. Covers SDNN vs RMSSD and the luteal-phase HRV decrease.
- [Resting heart rate](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/resting-heart-rate.html): How wearables derive overnight RHR and the well-evidenced few-bpm luteal-phase rise driven by progesterone.
- [Basal body temperature (BBT)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/basal-body-temperature.html): The progesterone-driven post-ovulatory temperature shift, oral BBT vs wrist skin temperature, and why temperature confirms ovulation after the fact.
- [Cervical mucus](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/cervical-mucus.html): Estrogen-driven mucus changes across the cycle, the observation-based logging method, and the research on mucus and the fertile window.
- [AMH (anti-Müllerian hormone)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/amh.html): What ovarian-reserve testing measures, why AMH is cycle-day-independent, and why it doesn't predict an individual's chances of conceiving.
- [Estradiol (E2)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/estradiol.html): The primary reproductive-years estrogen, its curve across the cycle, and serum vs urinary E3G testing.
- [TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/tsh.html): The pituitary-thyroid feedback loop, TSH's circadian rhythm, and population-level estrogen-thyroid crosstalk.
- [Ferritin](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/ferritin.html): The iron-storage protein behind iron panels and how menstrual blood loss relates to iron stores at the population level.
- [Wrist temperature](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/wrist-temperature.html): Wearable-measured skin temperature at the wrist, distinct from core or oral basal body temperature, tracked overnight against a rolling personal baseline.
- [Blood pressure](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/blood-pressure.html): The force blood exerts against artery walls, reported as systolic over diastolic pressure in millimeters of mercury.
- [Respiratory rate](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/respiratory-rate.html): Breaths per minute, set by a brainstem breathing center that responds to blood oxygen, carbon dioxide, and pH.
- [SpO2 (blood oxygen saturation)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/spo2.html): The percentage of hemoglobin carrying oxygen, estimated by wearables using red and infrared light at the wrist or fingertip, usually overnight.
- [VO2 max](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/vo2-max.html): The highest rate at which the body takes in, transports, and uses oxygen during intense exercise, reflecting combined heart, lung, and muscle capacity.
- [Blood glucose](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/blood-glucose.html): The concentration of glucose circulating in the bloodstream, regulated mainly by insulin and glucagon.
- [Sleep stages](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/sleep-stages.html): The recurring light, deep, and REM sleep phases wearables estimate overnight, cycling roughly every 90 to 110 minutes.
- [HRV: RMSSD](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/hrv-rmssd.html): The root mean square of successive differences between heartbeats, the primary time-domain HRV measure and the one most consumer wearables report.
- [Heart rate](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/heart-rate.html): Beats per minute set by the heart's own pacemaker, adjusted by the autonomic nervous system and hormones with movement, stress, and rest.
- [Body temperature](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/body-temperature.html): The heat level the hypothalamus regulates, covering core vs. skin vs. oral measurement, circadian rhythm, and the revised 98.6°F average.
- [Step count](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/steps.html): Daily steps counted by an accelerometer, and where accuracy breaks down.
- [Active energy (calories burned)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/active-energy.html): Calories burned through movement, estimated by wearables from motion and heart-rate data separately from resting energy.
- [Sleep latency (time to fall asleep)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/sleep-latency.html): How long it takes to fall asleep, measured in a lab from lights out to the first scored epoch of sleep and estimated by wearables from movement and heart rate.
- [LH surge](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/lh-surge.html): The rapid rise in luteinizing hormone triggered once estradiol peaks, signaling the ovary to release an egg roughly 34 to 36 hours later.
- [Luteal phase](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/luteal-phase.html): The second half of the menstrual cycle, from ovulation until the next period, driven by progesterone from the corpus luteum.
- [Follicular phase](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/follicular-phase.html): The first half of the menstrual cycle, from day one of the period until ovulation.
- [Ovulation](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/ovulation.html): The release of a mature egg from an ovarian follicle roughly midway through the cycle, triggered by the LH surge, after which the emptied follicle becomes the corpus luteum.
- [Fertile window](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/fertile-window.html): The roughly six-day stretch of the cycle when intercourse can lead to conception, ending on ovulation day, shaped by sperm survival time.
- [Ovulation test (OPK)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/ovulation-test-opk.html): A urine strip that detects the LH surge before ovulation, and why a positive predicts but doesn't confirm ovulation.
- [Cycle length](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/cycle-length.html): The number of days from day 1 of one period through the day before the next, with real-world data on the distribution.
- [Period flow](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/period-flow.html): The amount of menstrual bleeding, usually logged as light, medium, or heavy, and how researchers measure blood loss directly.
- [Spotting & intermenstrual bleeding](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/spotting-intermenstrual-bleeding.html): Light vaginal bleeding between periods, logged separately from period flow so it doesn't reset the cycle-day count.
- [Menstrual phase](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/menstrual-phase.html): The days of bleeding that open each cycle, triggered by progesterone withdrawal, and why apps label it separately from the follicular phase.
- [Cervical position](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/cervical-position.html): A fertility awareness check on cervix height, firmness, and opening, which shifts higher, softer, and more open around the fertile window.
- [Anovulatory cycle](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/anovulatory-cycle.html): A cycle in which no egg is released, so no corpus luteum forms and progesterone never rises the way it does in an ovulatory cycle.
- [Progesterone](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/progesterone.html): The hormone the corpus luteum makes after ovulation, tested by blood draw or urine, that supports the luteal phase.
- [FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/fsh.html): The pituitary hormone that recruits ovarian follicles each cycle, and why blood testing conventions call for an early-follicular draw.
- [Testosterone](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/testosterone.html): Where women's testosterone comes from, how labs report total vs. free testosterone, and what research shows about changes across the cycle.
- [Free testosterone](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/free-testosterone.html): The small unbound share of testosterone in blood, how labs calculate it from total testosterone and SHBG.
- [SHBG (sex hormone-binding globulin)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/shbg.html): The liver-made protein that binds testosterone and estradiol in blood, affecting how much stays free and active.
- [Cortisol](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/cortisol.html): The adrenal hormone behind the HPA axis, with a strong daily rhythm, and how serum, saliva, and urine tests differ.
- [Prolactin](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/prolactin.html): The pituitary hormone behind milk production, how dopamine keeps it in check, and why it rises.
- [DHEA-S (dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/dhea-s.html): The sulfated form of DHEA, an adrenal androgen precursor, and how it's tested.
- [Insulin](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/insulin.html): The pancreatic hormone that moves glucose into cells, and what a fasting insulin test measures via lab draw.
- [Estrone (E1)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/estrone.html): One of the three main estrogens, made largely in fat tissue, and why it becomes the body's main estrogen after menopause.
- [Free T4 (free thyroxine)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/free-t4.html): The unbound, biologically active portion of thyroxine, the thyroid gland's main secreted hormone, usually tested alongside TSH.
- [Free T3 (free triiodothyronine)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/free-t3.html): The small unbound fraction of T3, the biologically active thyroid hormone, most of which comes from tissue conversion of T4.
- [Reverse T3 (rT3)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/reverse-t3.html): An inactive form of thyroid hormone produced when deiodinase enzymes break down T4, and why clinical reviews report it hasn't proven useful in routine care.
- [Thyroid antibodies (TPO & thyroglobulin antibodies)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/thyroid-antibodies.html): Immune proteins targeting thyroid peroxidase and thyroglobulin, the standard blood-draw markers of thyroid autoimmunity.
- [hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/hcg.html): The placental hormone that sustains the corpus luteum's progesterone output in early pregnancy and that pregnancy tests detect in urine or blood.
- [PdG (pregnanediol glucuronide)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/pdg.html): The urinary metabolite of progesterone, used to confirm ovulation happened without a blood draw.
- [E3G (estrone-3-glucuronide)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/e3g.html): A urinary breakdown product of estradiol that tracks the serum estrogen curve, read by at-home fertility monitors.
- [17-OH progesterone (17-hydroxyprogesterone)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/17-oh-progesterone.html): A steroid intermediate on the pathway from progesterone toward cortisol, measured by blood draw in certain adrenal and fertility workups.
- [Androstenedione](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/androstenedione.html): An androgen made by the ovaries and adrenal glands that peripheral tissues convert into testosterone and, via aromatase, into estrone.
- [Fasting glucose](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/fasting-glucose.html): The concentration of glucose in the blood after at least eight hours without food, drawn as a lab test and used as a baseline reading on standard metabolic panels.
- [HbA1c (hemoglobin A1c)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/hba1c.html): The share of hemoglobin with glucose attached, reflecting average blood glucose over roughly the past three months.
- [C-peptide](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/c-peptide.html): A short protein chain the pancreas releases in equal amounts alongside insulin, measured by lab blood draw.
- [Creatinine](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/creatinine.html): A muscle waste product filtered out by the kidneys, measured by serum blood draw as a standard part of routine bloodwork and kidney function estimates.
- [BUN (blood urea nitrogen)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/bun.html): The amount of urea nitrogen in the blood, a liver-made waste product filtered out by the kidneys, measured on routine panels like the basic metabolic panel.
- [eGFR (estimated glomerular filtration rate)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/egfr.html): A calculated estimate of how fast the kidneys filter blood, derived from a serum creatinine result plus age and sex using a standard equation.
- [ALT (alanine aminotransferase)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/alt.html): A liver enzyme that leaks into the blood when liver cells are stressed or damaged, measured by standard blood draw.
- [AST (aspartate aminotransferase)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/ast.html): An enzyme found mainly in the liver but also the heart, skeletal muscle, kidneys, and red blood cells, released into blood when those cells are damaged.
- [Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/alkaline-phosphatase.html): An enzyme made mainly in the liver and bone, with smaller amounts from the intestine and, during pregnancy, the placenta, measured on liver or metabolic panels.
- [Bilirubin (total & direct)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/bilirubin.html): A yellow pigment made when the body breaks down heme from retired red blood cells, reported as total and direct fractions on a liver panel.
- [Total cholesterol](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/total-cholesterol.html): The combined amount of cholesterol in the blood, counting the cholesterol carried by HDL, LDL, and VLDL particles, measured on a standard lipid panel.
- [HDL cholesterol](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/hdl.html): The cholesterol carried inside high-density lipoprotein particles, the smallest and densest of the particles that move fats through the bloodstream.
- [LDL cholesterol](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/ldl.html): The cholesterol carried by low-density lipoprotein, the particle that delivers most of the cholesterol circulating in blood to tissues around the body.
- [Triglycerides](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/triglycerides.html): A fat molecule built from one glycerol backbone joined to three fatty acids, the body's main form of stored and transported fat, measured on a lipid panel.
- [ApoB (apolipoprotein B)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/apob.html): The main structural protein of LDL, VLDL, and related lipoprotein particles, with one ApoB molecule per particle, measured by blood draw.
- [Lipoprotein(a)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/lipoprotein-a.html): A cholesterol-carrying particle built like an LDL particle with an extra protein, apolipoprotein(a), bonded to its surface, measured on extended lipid panels.
- [Hemoglobin](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/hemoglobin.html): The iron-containing protein inside red blood cells that carries oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body, reported as part of a complete blood count.
- [Hematocrit](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/hematocrit.html): The fraction of blood volume taken up by red blood cells, reported as a percentage as part of a complete blood count.
- [Red blood cell (RBC) count](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/red-blood-cells.html): The number of red blood cells, the body's oxygen-carrying cells, in a set volume of blood, measured as part of a complete blood count.
- [White blood cell (WBC) count](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/white-blood-cells.html): The number of white blood cells, the cells of the immune system, in a set volume of blood, reported as part of a complete blood count with a differential.
- [Platelet count](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/platelets.html): The number of platelets, small cell fragments made by bone marrow that clump to stop bleeding, in a set volume of blood.
- [MCV (mean corpuscular volume)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/mcv.html): The average size of red blood cells, one of the red cell indices reported as part of a complete blood count.
- [Serum iron](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/serum-iron.html): The iron circulating in blood bound to transferrin, measured by blood draw, and why it swings within a single day.
- [TIBC & transferrin saturation](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/tibc-transferrin-saturation.html): How much iron the blood's carrier proteins can hold (TIBC) and the share of that capacity currently in use (transferrin saturation).
- [hs-CRP (high-sensitivity C-reactive protein)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/hs-crp.html): A high-sensitivity blood test for C-reactive protein, a liver-made marker of inflammation, and how it differs from standard CRP.
- [ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/esr.html): How far red blood cells settle in a tube of blood over one hour, an older, less specific inflammation marker than CRP.
- [Homocysteine](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/homocysteine.html): An amino acid produced during methionine metabolism, kept in check by B12, folate, and B6, and what large B-vitamin trials found when it was lowered.
- [Vitamin D (25-hydroxyvitamin D)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/vitamin-d.html): The standard blood test for vitamin D status, measuring the storage form of the vitamin rather than its active hormone form.
- [Vitamin B12](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/b12.html): A cobalt-containing vitamin the body needs for DNA synthesis and red blood cell formation, and how blood levels are tested.
- [Folate (vitamin B9)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/folate.html): The B vitamin behind DNA synthesis and new cell formation, the difference between folate and folic acid, and how lab results are measured.
- [Vitamin A (retinol)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/vitamin-a.html): A fat-soluble vitamin measured on lab panels as serum retinol, and what the blood test shows.
- [Zinc](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/zinc.html): An essential trace mineral behind hundreds of enzymes with no dedicated body store, and the limits of a serum zinc test.
- [Urinalysis](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/urinalysis.html): The standard urine test, done three ways: a visual color check, a chemical dipstick, and a microscope exam of the sediment.
- [Urine hormone metabolites](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/urine-hormone-metabolites.html): Urinary cortisol, melatonin's breakdown product aMT6s, and the DNA-oxidation marker 8-OHdG, and how each is measured in urine.
- [Hot flashes](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/hot-flashes.html): A sudden wave of heat felt across the face, neck, and chest, often with sweating and flushed skin, typically lasting one to five minutes. Linked to changing estrogen levels and a narrowed thermoneutral zone, most often during the menopause transition.
- [Night sweats](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/night-sweats.html): Episodes of heavy sweating during sleep, sharing the same vasomotor physiology as hot flashes. Commonly reported during the menopause transition but also found across many other populations and life stages.
- [Menstrual cramps (dysmenorrhea)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/cramps-dysmenorrhea.html): Crampy lower-abdominal pain around the start of a period, driven by prostaglandins that make the uterus contract. Pain typically begins within hours of bleeding, peaks in the first day or two, and eases within about three days.
- [Bloating](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/bloating.html): A feeling of abdominal fullness, pressure, or visible swelling noticed at points in the menstrual cycle. Linked to cyclic fluid retention that peaks on the first day of flow and to slower gut transit during the luteal phase.
- [Breast tenderness](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/breast-tenderness.html): Soreness, heaviness, or aching in breast tissue. When it follows the cycle it's called cyclical mastalgia, the most common type of breast pain, usually building during the luteal phase as hormone shifts cause lobule enlargement and stromal edema, then easing with menstruation.
- [Fatigue](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/fatigue.html): A feeling of tiredness or low energy that doesn't fully lift with rest, with many possible causes. Logged as a daily symptom because it's one of the most commonly reported premenstrual symptoms in studies of healthy menstruating women.
- [Mood swings](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/mood-swings.html): Noticeable shifts in emotional state over hours or days, logged as a subjective symptom. Surveys rank mood symptoms among the most common premenstrual complaints, though prospective daily-record studies find mood tracks the cycle less tightly than memory suggests.
- [Nausea](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/nausea.html): The queasy, unsettled stomach sensation that can precede vomiting, produced by brain circuits integrating signals from the gut, inner ear, cortex, and bloodstream. Logged as a subjective symptom across everyday, cycle-related, and early-pregnancy contexts.
- [Vaginal discharge](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/discharge.html): The normal fluid the vagina produces day to day, ranging from clear to white and watery to slightly thick. Its amount and texture shift across the menstrual cycle and it's logged as a simple daily observation.
- [Hirsutism](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/hirsutism.html): Growth of coarse, pigmented terminal hair in body areas where hair growth depends on androgens, such as the face, chest, and abdomen. Reflects the interaction between circulating androgen levels and how sensitive each hair follicle is to those hormones.
- [Hormonal acne](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/acne-hormonal.html): Acne that tracks with hormone shifts, driven by androgen receptors in sebaceous glands that stimulate growth and oil output. Many women report their acne flares before their period.
- [Hair thinning](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/hair-thinning.html): A drop in visible hair density on the scalp, occurring when fewer follicles are growing at once or when hairs shed faster than new ones replace them. Each follicle cycles through a growth phase (anagen), a short transition, and a resting phase (telogen).
- [Libido (sex drive)](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/libido-sex-drive.html): A person's overall level of sexual desire, shaped by hormones, stress, sleep, and life context. In menstruating people it often varies across the cycle, with several studies reporting a rise in desire around the middle of the cycle near ovulation.
- [Headaches & migraine](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/headache-migraine.html): Among the most commonly logged cycle symptoms. In people who menstruate, migraine attacks cluster in the days just before and during menstruation as estrogen falls sharply, a pattern called menstrual migraine that affects roughly 20 to 25 percent of women with migraine.
- [Insomnia](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/insomnia.html): Difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or getting sleep that feels restful despite enough time in bed, with next-day effects. As a logged symptom it captures how sleep felt, and self-reported sleep quality often dips around menstruation.
- [Heart palpitations](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/heart-palpitations.html): The felt awareness of your own heartbeat, described as fast, slow, regular, irregular, a flutter, a pound, or a skipped beat. Names the sensation itself rather than any single heart rhythm, so it's recorded as a symptom rather than a measurement.
- [Cold intolerance](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/cold-intolerance.html): An unusual sensitivity to a cold environment or cold temperatures, feeling cold when others are comfortable or needing extra layers to feel warm. A reported sensation rather than a temperature reading, so it's logged as a symptom, not measured by a device.
- [Restless legs](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/restless-legs.html): An urge to move the legs that starts at rest, often with uncomfortable sensations that ease with movement and tend to be worse in the evening or at night. Researchers estimate restless legs syndrome affects between 5% and 15% of the population.
- [Mindful minutes](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/mindful-minutes.html): The Apple Health metric that counts time logged in meditation or breathing sessions. It records that you practiced, not how the session went.
- [Fetal Heart Rate](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/fetal-heart-rate.html): The fetal heartbeat rate measured by Doppler or ultrasound at prenatal visits, logged from appointments.
- [Fundal Height](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/fundal-height.html): The tape measurement from pubic bone to the top of the uterus, recorded at prenatal checkups.
- [Antral Follicle Count](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/follicle-count.html): The number of small ovarian follicles counted on early-cycle ultrasound, an ovarian-reserve marker alongside AMH.
- [Endometrial Thickness](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/endometrial-thickness.html): The ultrasound measurement of the uterine lining, tracked in IVF and embryo-transfer cycles.
- [Embryo Grading](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/embryo-grading.html): The lab notation describing an embryo's appearance at day 3 or day 5, as reported by an IVF clinic.
- [IVF Cycle Numbers](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/encyclopedia/ivf-cycle-numbers.html): The counts recorded through an IVF cycle: eggs retrieved, mature, fertilized, and embryos developing.

## Condition tracking (what the app does, per condition)

- [Cycle syncing app](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/cycle-syncing-app.html): Phase detection and phase-tagged logging of workouts, meals, mood, sleep, and energy, with correlations drawn from your own logged history rather than textbook phase prescriptions.
- [PCOS tracker](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/pcos-tracker.html): Irregular-cycle handling, symptom and metabolic tracking, lab and bloodwork import (TSH, AMH, progesterone), and glucose support via Dexcom and Libre.
- [Endometriosis tracker](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/endometriosis-tracker.html): Pain and flare logging, symptom-to-phase correlations, and doctor-ready records to bring to appointments.
- [Perimenopause tracker](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/perimenopause-tracker.html): Hot flash and symptom logging, cycle-change monitoring as the pattern shifts, and patterns showing which weeks make symptoms worse.
- [IVF tracker](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/ivf-tracker.html): Medication, appointment, and protocol logging with hormone and lab values tracked over time. Does not include medication barcode scanning, injection site rotation, or clinic EMR sync.
- [PMDD tracker](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/pmdd-tracker.html): Daily charting of PMDD mood and physical symptoms against the cycle across two cycles, producing the pattern record a diagnosis conversation needs.
- [Postpartum tracker](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/postpartum-tracker.html): Bleeding, mood, sleep, and pain tracking through the fourth trimester, transitioning into cycle tracking when the period returns.
- [What's your wellness type?](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/wellness-type.html): Six wellness types read from your own last 30 days of sleep, movement, mood, and cycle data. Not a questionnaire — it is computed from logged data.

## Free tools

- [Tools index](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/tools/): All free women's health calculators.
- [Period calculator](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/tools/period-calculator.html): Predict your next period date.
- [Ovulation calculator](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/tools/ovulation-calculator.html): Predict your fertile window and ovulation day.
- [Due date calculator](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/tools/due-date-calculator.html): Calculate your pregnancy due date from LMP or conception date.
- [Pregnancy week calculator](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/tools/pregnancy-week-calculator.html): Find your current pregnancy week and trimester.
- [Cycle length calculator](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/tools/cycle-length-calculator.html): Calculate your average cycle length.
- [PMS & luteal phase calculator](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/tools/pms-calculator.html): Estimate when PMS symptoms are likely to start and map your luteal phase.
- [Sleep calculator](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/tools/sleep-calculator.html): Find your best bedtime or wake time using 90-minute sleep cycles, and see your sleep debt.
- [Caffeine calculator](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/tools/caffeine-calculator.html): Calculate the latest time to have caffeine and still sleep well.
- [Heart rate zone calculator](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/tools/heart-rate-zone-calculator.html): Find your zone 2 heart rate and training zones using the Gulati formula for women.
- [Protein calculator](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/tools/protein-calculator.html): Find your daily protein range in grams from your weight, activity level, and life stage.
- [Cycle phase calculator](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/tools/cycle-phase-calculator.html): Find out what phase of your menstrual cycle you're in today — menstrual, follicular, ovulatory, or luteal.
- [Creatine dosage calculator](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/tools/creatine-calculator.html): Calculate your creatine dose from your bodyweight, including maintenance and loading grams per day.
- [Macro calculator](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/tools/macro-calculator.html): Calculate your daily calories and macros, with separate follicular and luteal targets.
- [BMI calculator](https://www.go-go-gaia.com/tools/bmi-calculator.html): Get your BMI paired with waist-to-height ratio and what the number can't tell you, including context for PCOS and fertility.
